Ray marching time is reduced proportionally to the fraction of skipped macrocells [S2].

The claim states that time is reduced 'proportionally' to the fraction of skipped macrocells. The evidence shows that while rendering time decreases as the number of skipped macrocells increases (e.g., in the MRI dataset), the relationship is not strictly proportional. For instance, in the MRI dataset, increasing skipped macrocells from 0 to 167 reduces time by 1.57 ms, while increasing from 1,019 to 1,190 (a similar increment of 171) reduces time by 2.21 ms. Additionally, the evidence explicitly states that performance can degrade or worsen if the fraction of skipped cells is small (e.g., Engine dataset) or if overhead dominates (e.g., Agulhas dataset), contradicting a simple proportional reduction model where more skips always yield proportional time savings.
